summary: A 1976 note on out-of-band control signals in a host-to-host protocol, meaning urgent signals that travel separately from the main stream of data. It is historic and was obsoleted by RFC 7805.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like shouting a stop signal over the noise of a conversation. This note asked how computers can send that kind of urgent message.

questions: urgent data in host to host protocol
subtitle: Methods for sending urgent control signals independently from data in a host-to-host protocol.

tldr.problem: TCP mixes data and control signals on the same channel, meaning urgent interrupt signals get stuck behind data flow control mechanisms and cannot be delivered reliably.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 721 proposes using a separate interrupt channel with its own sequence number space, allowing interrupts to bypass data flow control and be reliably delivered one-at-a-time.
tldr.outcome: The design addresses the fundamental conflict between flow control and urgent signaling, providing a framework for reliable out-of-band communication.

facts.label: Delivery guarantee
facts.value: Exactly one copy per interrupt sent

today: RFC 721 is Historic. It was obsoleted by RFC 7805.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 721 addresses the problem of sending reliable out-of-band control signals (interrupts) in a host-to-host protocol. The TCP protocol combines data and controls on a single channel and uses flow control to manage data transmission. When an interrupt arrives, it must be flushed around the flow control mechanism, and the receiver may not get it reliably. The ARPANET protocol, while not reliable, separates interrupt and data channels, offering an alternative model.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP treats important control messages the same as regular data, so they can get stuck waiting for the data channel to clear. This proposal explains why that is a problem.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
sections.content: A reliable interrupt system must ensure that exactly one interrupt is delivered for each interrupt sent. The interrupt signal must be independent of data flow control—it must arrive whether or not buffers are available for data. The protocol need not provide order among multiple interrupts, but the interrupt should not interfere with the reliable delivery of other data and controls. Synchronization between interrupt and data channels can be left to the user layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Urgent messages must get through, not get stuck behind regular data. You only need one copy of each message, not necessarily in order.

sections.title: Implementation Approach
sections.content: To provide reliable delivery and identify interrupts, a separate sequence number space is required. A separate interrupt channel makes interrupts independent of flow control. For TCP with multiple channels, one approach couples all channels to channel zero's sequence numbers, with each interrupt carrying both a channel-zero sequence number (for duplicate detection from old connections) and its own sequence number (for ordering within the interrupt stream).
sections.plainLanguage: Each urgent message gets a number so the receiver knows which ones arrived and which are duplicates from old connections.
